analysis.one_liner: Banned new federal permits and leases for mining on public lands.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it was referred to a House subcommittee and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped the federal government from issuing any new permits, leases, or renewals for mining on federal land, with exceptions for operations already authorized and for national security. Mining on land the government already owned would continue under existing permits until those permits ran out. The bill was referred to a subcommittee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who use federal public lands for recreation, drinking water, fishing, and hunting would gain, because new mining operations on federal land often bring water pollution, habitat loss, and cleanup liabilities. Taxpayers would also gain, since federal land mining has historically been governed by the 1872 Mining Law, which lets companies extract hardrock minerals without paying royalties and can leave reclamation costs to the public.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Recreational users of public lands and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: The bill barred any new federal permits, leases, or renewals for mining on federal land, with exceptions only for existing authorizations and national security.

By freezing new mining authorizations, it would have prevented additional land disturbance, water pollution, and the long-term cleanup burdens that mining projects can leave to taxpayers when companies fold.

analysis.who_pays: Mining companies would lose access to future federal land opportunities, and mining-dependent communities could lose future jobs. Some argue consumers could face higher prices for domestically supplied minerals if supply tightened.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium covers all mineral activities on federal land, including reclamation (cleanup) work, which could slow restoration of already-damaged sites and is a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.
Existing permits could not be renewed even after the current activity ended, which eventually shut down lawful operations and the jobs tied to them, a real cost to mining communities.
Critics could fairly argue the bill was overbroad: a blanket stop rather than environmental conditions, bonding requirements, or royalty reforms that would let carefully regulated projects proceed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have preserved federal land and protected watersheds from new mining, but it was a blunt instrument: a blanket moratorium, with no new permits even where a project could meet modern environmental standards, and no reauthorization of existing permits even where cleanup was the purpose. A more tailored approach (higher royalties, stronger reclamation bonds) might have achieved similar protection with fewer drawbacks. As written, the environmental benefit was real but so was the economic cost, and the bill never had the support to seriously test either.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to a subcommittee of the House Resources Committee on July 28, 1999, no one else signed on, and it never came up again before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Wu introduced the bill on July 22, 1999, and it was referred to the House Resources Committee the same day.
Six days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it stayed.
No further action was taken before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, so the bill died without a vote.
No representative cosponsored the bill, which limited its chances of ever moving.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mining companies that wanted to develop federal land kept the ability to obtain new permits and leases unchanged, and the public lands remained open to them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Mining companies seeking federal land access

for.name: Rep. David Wu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the moratorium bill; it was his sole action beyond referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one sponsor and zero cosponsors, and no vote was ever recorded, so there was no discernible partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have ended new federal permits, leases, and renewals for hardrock mining on public land, cutting off future projects. Existing operations could continue but never renew their permits, so even incumbents would eventually lose access.
A freeze on new mines means fewer orders for equipment, drilling, and exploration services over time.
